title: [Top Question - Asked by Google, Microsoft, Amazon #48] Design an Ad Ranking / Click Prediction System at Scale - How It Actually Works
text:
Google Shows You an Ad in 8 Milliseconds — And It Just Beat 10,000 Other Ads to Get There
This is deep dive on how such systems are built and how it actually works —
Every ad you see on a search results page, a social feed, or a video pre-roll just won a real-time auction against thousands of competitors — decided, scored, and rendered in single-digit milliseconds. Underneath that one ad slot sits a multi-stage machine learning pipeline: candidate retrieval, click-probability prediction, bid scoring, an auction mechanism, and a feedback loop that retrains itself on the outcome of every impression. Get the click-probability estimate wrong by a few percentage points at scale, and you either bankrupt advertisers with wasted spend or leave billions of dollars of ad revenue on the table.
In this post wee design that system the way you’d actually be asked to in a senior/staff ML system-design interview or a real production planning doc: requirements first, then ML framing, then architecture, then every component torn open, then trade-offs, then “what breaks and how do we survive it.”

1. Clarifying Requirements
Before drawing a single box, we pin down what “good” means. An ad ranking system without explicit latency, revenue, and fairness targets is not a system — it’s a demo that will bankrupt someone’s ad budget on day one.
Functional Requirements
Ad request handling — given a user, a page/app context (search query, feed position, video), and a pool of eligible ads, return a ranked set of ads (typically 1–4 slots) to render, within the page-load critical path.
Click-through-rate (CTR) prediction — for every candidate ad in context, estimate the probability the user will click it (pCTR), which feeds directly into the auction.
Conversion-rate prediction (pCVR) — for advertisers bidding on conversions (purchases, sign-ups) rather than clicks, estimate probability of downstream conversion given a click, since the two are optimized differently and the second is far sparser data.
